summary: This informational document describes operational practices for running DNS with security extensions (DNSSEC), aimed at zone administrators. It covers key generation and storage, signature generation, key rollover and related policies. It replaced RFC 2541 and was itself replaced by RFC 6781.

eli5.summary: Signing DNS answers is like stamping letters with a special seal. This explains how to make and guard the seal and how to swap it for a new one safely.

subtitle: How to safely run and maintain DNS zones with security extensions.

tldr.problem: DNSSEC adds signatures to DNS answers so resolvers can verify they have not been tampered with. Running a signed zone requires careful management of cryptographic keys, signatures, and rollovers to avoid breaking the chain of trust.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes practices for generating and storing private keys securely, rolling over keys without losing verifiability, managing signature validity periods, and keeping the chain of trust intact during routine maintenance and emergency situations.
tldr.outcome: Clear operational practices help zone administrators maintain DNSSEC security without outages. The RFC was replaced by RFC 6781 with updated guidance on algorithms and key sizes.

today: RFC 4641 is an Informational RFC from September 2006 that was obsoleted by RFC 6781 in December 2012. It provided operational practices for DNSSEC zone administrators; RFC 6781 provides updated guidance reflecting changes in algorithm recommendations and key sizing.

sections.title: DNSSEC Operational Challenges
sections.content:
DNSSEC (Domain Name System Security Extensions) adds digital signatures to DNS answers so that verifying clients can confirm the data has not been modified in transit. This RFC is aimed at zone administrators who want to deploy DNSSEC and describes operational practices based on real-world experience from early deployments.

Operating a signed zone differs from operating an unsigned one. Zone administrators must manage cryptographic keys, generate and refresh signatures, and perform key rollovers while ensuring that the chain of trust from the root zone down to their zone remains intact. Mistakes can cause an entire zone to become invisible to security-aware resolvers.
sections.eli5: When you sign DNS answers with a secret stamp, you have to be careful to keep the stamp safe, keep the signatures fresh, and change the stamp safely without confusing the DNS system.

sections.title: Keeping the Chain of Trust Intact
sections.content:
DNSSEC works by creating a chain of trust from the root zone down through every parent zone to your zone. If any link in that chain is broken, security-aware resolvers mark your data as Bogus and refuse to use it. This can effectively make your zone invisible.

Zone administrators must coordinate with their parent zone (typically a registry) when exchanging or updating keys. During key compromises, administrators face a difficult choice: they can keep the chain of trust intact and risk allowing attacks with the compromised key, or they can deliberately break the chain and make their zone invisible until the compromise is resolved. Planning for these scenarios beforehand is essential.
sections.eli5: Your zone is part of a chain of trust from the root down to you. If the chain breaks, your domain disappears to security-aware clients. You need to work with your parent zone to keep the chain working.

sections.title: Key Generation and Storage
sections.content:
DNSSEC zones typically use two different types of keys. Key Signing Keys (KSKs) are strong keys that sign only the zone's key set; they change rarely and are carefully protected. Zone Signing Keys (ZSKs) sign all the zone's data and can be rolled over more frequently.

Keys should be generated offline on secure machines, not on networked systems. The RFC recommends a key effectivity period of about 13 months for KSKs (planning to replace them after 12 months) and about one month for ZSKs. Private keys must be protected from unauthorized access; the ideal setup keeps the zone master offline and uses a hidden master architecture for dynamic updates. Key sizes depend on the zone's value: the RFC suggests 1024 bits for low-value domains, 1300 bits for medium-value domains, and 2048 bits for high-value domains like the root zone.
sections.eli5: Make keys offline on safe computers. Keep the master copy offline if you can. Use strong keys for the root zone. Change your keys on a schedule so they do not get old and weak.

sections.title: Signature Timing and Key Rollover
sections.content:
DNSSEC introduces absolute time to the DNS through signature expiration. Signatures have an inception time and an expiration time, and resolvers reject signatures that have expired. Zone administrators must coordinate signature validity periods with their zone's TTL (Time to Live) values and with slave server refresh intervals to avoid creating query load spikes at expiration time.

Key rollovers come in two main varieties. For Zone Signing Key rollovers, no parent interaction is needed; administrators can use either a pre-publish strategy (where the new key is published before the old key is removed) or a double-signature strategy (where both keys sign all data during the transition). Key Signing Key rollovers require coordination with the parent zone and potentially with resolvers that have the key configured as a trust anchor. The RFC provides detailed timing guidance to prevent failures during maintenance.
sections.eli5: Signatures have an expiration date. Change them before they expire, but not too fast or you will overload your servers. When rolling keys, follow a plan so old and new keys both work during the switch.

sections.title: Security and Algorithm Guidance
sections.content:
The RFC recommends RSA with SHA-1 hashing as the preferred algorithm for DNSSEC at the time of publication. It notes that RSA's strength can be increased by using longer keys to defeat known attacks, and SHA-1 is preferred over MD5 because MD5 has known weaknesses. However, the RFC acknowledges that SHA-1 itself has cryptanalysis issues and recommends that implementations adopt stronger hash algorithms like SHA-256 as they become standardized.

The choice of algorithm, key size, and effectivity period must balance security against operational complexity. Very long key effectivity periods reduce the frequency of rollovers but increase the value of the key to attackers. Very short periods increase operational burden. For high-level zones like the root, the RFC recommends the strongest keys and most careful handling, including keeping the private key offline at all times.
sections.eli5: Use strong math to protect your keys. Keep important keys safer than less important ones. Change keys often enough to stay safe but not so often that you break the system.
